**User Interface Requirements**

The system shall provide a user-friendly and accessible web-based interface for the Principal and authorized teachers of Cambaog National High School (CNHS). The interface shall provide clear navigation, recognizable controls, and appropriate instructions to support essential functions, including uploading and managing the Official DepEd E-Class Record (ECR) and School Form 2 (SF2), viewing academic analytics, reviewing academic risk classifications and intervention recommendations, managing reading assessment records, and monitoring learner intervention progress.

The system shall provide role-based dashboards according to the responsibilities of authorized users. The Principal dashboard shall support school-level academic monitoring, learner performance analytics, academic risk monitoring, oversight of reading assessment completion and results, intervention management, lesson plan review, user management, and report generation. Meanwhile, the Teacher dashboard shall support class and learner record management, academic performance monitoring, identification of weak-performing subjects, review of academic risk classifications and Random Forest advisory predictions, recording and reviewing applicable Phil-IRI reading assessment results, preparation and review of draft Personalized Learning Plans (PLPs), intervention monitoring, and lesson plan submission.

The interface shall present academic information, reading assessment results, and intervention-related outputs in an organized and understandable manner to support academic monitoring and decision-making. Reading assessment and ARAL intervention monitoring shall remain distinct processes, with intervention decisions guided by applicable assessment results and established school procedures. Access to system functions shall be limited according to the assigned roles and permissions of the Principal and authorized teachers.

**Technical Requirements**

CNHS LEARN shall operate as a centralized web-based school data analytics system developed using HTML5, JavaScript/TypeScript, and the Next.js framework. Tailwind CSS shall be used for the design and styling of the user interface to support responsive layouts and consistent navigation across the system's modules.

The system shall utilize Supabase as its backend platform, with PostgreSQL serving as the centralized database for storing and managing learner academic records, attendance records, intervention records, user information, role assignments, and other relevant school data. Supabase Authentication shall support user authentication and account management, while role-based access control shall restrict access to authorized system functions and information.

The system shall support the importation and management of official academic and attendance records through supported file formats, including CSV and Excel (.xlsx). Academic information obtained from the Official DepEd E-Class Record (ECR), particularly finalized class-subject grades, shall serve as the primary basis for academic performance monitoring, academic risk classification, and identification of weak-performing subjects. Attendance records obtained from School Form 2 (SF2) shall be maintained separately for attendance monitoring and reporting.

The system shall implement rule-based academic risk classification using predefined criteria to categorize learners according to their recorded academic performance. Weak-performing subjects shall be identified through predefined grade-based conditions. These processes shall operate independently of the Random Forest model to maintain a consistent basis for official academic risk classification.

For supplementary academic analysis, the system shall integrate a trained Random Forest classification model implemented using Python and the scikit-learn library. The model shall utilize 13 numeric academic indicators to generate advisory academic risk predictions categorized as High Risk, Moderate Risk, or Low Risk. The trained classifier shall consist of 200 decision trees with a maximum tree depth of 12\. Its predictions shall serve as additional decision-support information and shall not override the official rule-based academic risk classification or independently determine learner interventions.

The system shall also implement rule-based intervention recommendation mechanisms that consider learners' academic performance, identified weak-performing subjects, and applicable assessment results. The Phil-IRI Group Screening Test (GST) shall serve as the initial reading screening for all applicable Grades 7–10 learners in English and Filipino, independently of their academic grades and academic risk classifications. Where indicated, individualized reading assessment results and established school procedures shall guide the determination of reading intervention needs and applicable ARAL qualification and placement. Learners experiencing academic difficulties in other learning areas may be considered for Classroom Remediation based on the review of authorized teachers.

The Personalized Learning Plan (PLP) component shall provide draft intervention guidance based on identified academic needs and applicable recommendations. These draft plans shall support teacher review, modification, finalization, and intervention monitoring. The system shall not automatically generate complete lesson plans, instructional modules, or learning materials. Final decisions regarding intervention activities and implementation shall remain the responsibility of authorized school personnel.

The web application shall be deployed and hosted using Vercel, while GitHub shall be utilized for source code management and version control throughout system development.

**Performance Requirements**

The system shall support the efficient processing, storage, retrieval, and presentation of academic and attendance information within a centralized web-based environment. The uploading and processing of Official DepEd E-Class Record (ECR) and School Form 2 (SF2) files shall be performed within reasonable response times under normal operating conditions.

The system shall efficiently execute its core monitoring and decision-support functions, including academic record processing, identification of weak-performing subjects, rule-based academic risk classification, Random Forest advisory prediction, rule-based intervention recommendation, recording and retrieval of applicable reading assessment results, learner intervention monitoring, and report generation.

The system shall support simultaneous access by multiple authorized users while maintaining acceptable responsiveness and operational stability. Academic analytics, dashboards, and monitoring functions shall retrieve and present available information without unnecessary delays that could interfere with routine school activities.

**Security Requirements**

The system shall implement Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) to regulate access to system functions and information according to the responsibilities of authorized users. The Principal and teachers shall be assigned appropriate access permissions to ensure that administrative functions, academic records, intervention information, and reporting features are accessible only to authorized personnel.

The system shall implement authentication and authorization mechanisms through Supabase Authentication to verify user identities and manage access to protected system functions. User credentials and authenticated sessions shall be protected against unauthorized access.

Access to learners' academic records, attendance information, academic risk classifications, intervention records, and Personalized Learning Plans (PLPs) shall be restricted according to assigned user roles and permissions. Teachers shall be limited to the academic and intervention information necessary for their authorized responsibilities, while the Principal shall have access to school-level management and monitoring functions.

The system shall implement appropriate access controls to protect stored learner information against unauthorized viewing, modification, disclosure, or misuse. These controls shall support the confidentiality and integrity of school records maintained within the centralized database.

The operational system shall be intended for the Principal and authorized teachers. Student access shall not form part of the system's operational user roles, consistent with the defined scope and limitations of the study.

**Table 5\. A. Functional Requirements **

| ID | Functional Requirement | Description |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | Import Official School Records | The system shall allow authorized users to upload the Official DepEd E-Class Record (ECR) and Official School Form 2 (SF2) in supported Excel or CSV formats, where applicable. |
| 2 | Academic Data Extraction and Mapping | The system shall retrieve and map learner information, class-subject records, and finalized grades from the uploaded Official DepEd E-Class Record (ECR) and store the extracted academic data in the system database. |
| 3 | Centralized Data Storage | The system shall store learner profiles, academic records, and attendance records in a centralized repository while maintaining separate processes for academic data and attendance data.  |
| 4 | Data Validation | The system shall validate uploaded academic and attendance records for completeness, consistency, and format correctness before accepting and processing the data. |
| 5 | Academic Risk Classification | The system shall classify learners as High Risk, Moderate Risk, or Low Risk based on finalized class-subject grades from the Official DepEd E-Class Record (ECR) using the predefined grade-based: below 75 for High Risk, 75–80 for Moderate Risk, and above 80 for Low Risk. Learners without finalized class-subject grades shall not automatically be classified as High Risk. |
| 6 | Academic Analysis and Intervention Recommendation  | The system shall use Random Forest to provide supplementary, advisory analysis of learners’ academic performance and identified weak-performing subjects to support intervention recommendations. Random Forest shall not determine or override the official academic risk classification, which is based on the predefined grade-based. |
| 7 | Personalized Learning Plan (PLP) | The system shall generate draft Personalized Learning Plan (PLP) suggestions based on the learner’s academic performance, official academic risk classification, identified weak-performing subjects, and recommended interventions. Authorized teachers and the Principal shall be able to review, modify, personalize, and finalize the suggestions. The system shall not automatically generate complete lesson plans, instructional units, or learning materials. |
| 8 | Intervention Monitoring | The system shall enable authorised teachers, as well as the Principal, to make observations related to interventions and track intervention implementation and progress. |
| 9 | Report Generation | The system shall generate academic reports, analytics dashboards, attendance reports, intervention recommendations, PLP information, and intervention monitoring reports according to the authenticated user’s access permissions. |
| 10 | User Authentication and Role-Based Access Control | The system shall offer user authentication and role-based access control (RBAC) to limit system functions and learner information based on the authenticated user's role.   |
| 11 | Reading Assessment Management | The system shall support the recording, importation, and review of applicable Phil-IRI reading assessment results for Grades 7 to 10 learners in English and Filipino. Initial GST screening shall be managed independently of academic risk classifications, while individualized assessment results, where applicable, shall support reading intervention decisions based on established school procedures |

**Table 6\. B. Non-Functional Requirements**  
These requirements describe the quality of the system, including the performance, usability, security, and reliability. 

| Category | Requirement | Description |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Usability | User-Friendly Interface | The system shall be designed to have a user friendly interface to enable the authorised functions of the Principal and teachers. |
| Performance  | Fast Processing | Under normal operating conditions, the system shall process data uploaded and data requests for the system in reasonable time. |
| Security | Role-Based Access Control | The system shall limit access to system functions and learner information based upon the user's assigned role.  |
| Reliability | System Stability | The system shall operate consistently under normal conditions and minimize unexpected failures that could interrupt authorized users' access to essential functions. |
| Compatibility | Browser Support | The system shall run on compatible Web browsers. |
| Scalability | Expandable System | The system shall support future increases in the number of learner records, authorized users, and academic monitoring activities through appropriate expansion of its data storage and application resources. |
| Maintainability | Easy Updates | The system shall support maintenance, updates, and modifications to its software components and functions without unnecessarily disrupting existing system operations. |

**Design of Software, Systems and Process**  
Design of software, systems and process refers to the process of designing technologies that operate effectively and efficiently. This is done through the design of dependable software, organization of system parts, and workflow design to allow for effective development and functioning.  
   
**Context Diagram \- on going**   
A context diagram gives an overview of the system by indicating how the system operates with other entities such as the principal, teachers, and students. The context diagram shows the flow of data into and out of the system as well as the responses of the system.  
![][image25]  
**Figure 25\. Context Diagram**  
Figure 25 presents the context diagram of CNHS LEARN, illustrating the interaction between the centralized school data analytics system and its two primary external entities: the School Principal and Teachers. Teachers provide academic records, attendance information, reading assessment results, intervention updates, and lesson plan submissions. In return, the system provides academic performance analysis, academic risk classifications, draft personalized intervention recommendations, learner progress information, attendance reports, and lesson plan review status.  
The School Principal provides user and school management information, lesson plan review and approval data, and monitoring or report requests. The system responds by presenting academic analytics, intervention and progress information, attendance and system reports, and lesson plan submission information.  
Overall, the context diagram illustrates how CNHS Learn serves as a centralized platform for managing learner information, academic analytics, assessment data, attendance, intervention recommendations and monitoring, and other academic processes. The diagram focuses on the information exchanged between the users and the system, while internal processes such as data validation, rule-based processing, Random Forest analysis, assessment interpretation, and intervention routing are performed within CNHS LEARN and are therefore not represented as separate processes in the context diagram.

It identifies the School Principal and teachers as the primary system actors and presents the functions available to each role, including academic record management, academic monitoring, intervention management, lesson plan processing, attendance monitoring, and report generation. The diagram provides an overview of the system's functional scope and role-based interactions, serving as a reference for the design and implementation of its major features.

 The system has to meet the following user group needs:

The School Principal can manage user accounts, enable or disable accounts, manage classes and sections, view academic records and analytics, review lesson plans and ARAL referrals, amonitor ARAL assessments and outcomes, monitor learner interventions and attendance, and generate school-wide reports.

The Teacher can upload ECR and SF2 records, which are validated by the system and submit lesson plans. The Teacher can also record learner attendance, view academic records, academic risk classifications, weak-performing subjects, and review rule-based recommendations. **Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN)**

The BPMN diagrams present the workflows performed by the School Principal and authorized teachers, showing how they access and utilize the system's functions according to their assigned roles and responsibilities.

The diagrams illustrate the processes involved in managing academic records, monitoring learner performance, reviewing academic risk information and intervention recommendations, managing reading-related interventions, monitoring attendance, processing lesson plans, and generating reports. These workflows also demonstrate how the system supports school personnel in performing academic monitoring and intervention-related activities while maintaining role-based access to learner information.

The following BPMN diagrams present the operational workflows of the Principal and Teacher modules, respectively, providing a visual representation of how the system's major functions are accessed and carried out.

**Principal BPMN**  
**![][image27]**  
**Figure 27\. Principal BPMN**

Figure 27 illustrates the School Principal's workflow in CNHS LEARN, focusing on school-wide academic monitoring, reading assessment oversight, intervention monitoring, lesson plan review, and report generation. The process begins when the School Principal logs into the system and accesses the Principal Dashboard, which provides access to the available monitoring and management modules.

In the Academic Monitoring module, the School Principal selects the appropriate school year, grade level, section, or other available filters to review academic performance information derived from validated Electronic Class Record (ECR) data. The system presents current-term academic risk classifications based on predefined academic risk classification criteria, together with information on weak-performing subjects and learners who may require additional academic support. The School Principal may also review available advisory Random Forest predictions of learners' academic risk levels for individual subjects in the succeeding grading term. These predictions are presented separately from actual academic results to support monitoring and planning without replacing the rule-based classifications.

For reading monitoring, the School Principal reviews available Group Screening Test (GST) results, individual reading assessment records, and learners' reading progress across the BOSY, MOSY, and EOSY assessment periods. This allows the School Principal to monitor reading assessment coverage, identify learners requiring continued support, and review the progress of reading-related intervention activities. Reading assessment outcomes and applicable intervention decisions remain based on the relevant assessment evidence and school procedures.

The workflow also includes Lesson Plan Management, where the School Principal reviews lesson plans submitted by teachers. The School Principal may approve a submitted lesson plan or return it with feedback for revision. When a lesson plan is returned, the Teacher may make the necessary corrections and resubmit it for another review. In addition, the School Principal can generate and review authorized school-level reports to support academic monitoring, instructional supervision, and decision-making.

Overall, the workflow demonstrates how CNHS LEARN provides the School Principal with centralized access to academic performance information, reading assessment records, intervention monitoring data, and instructional documents. Through these functions, the system supports school-wide monitoring and supervisory decision-making while maintaining the responsibilities of teachers in managing learner records and implementing appropriate interventions.

**Teacher BPMN**

![][image28]  
**Figure 28\. Teacher Flowchart**  
	Figure 28 illustrates the Teacher's workflow in CNHS LEARN, which covers academic record management, academic performance monitoring, reading assessment, intervention monitoring, lesson plan submission, and report generation. The process begins when the Teacher logs into the system and accesses the Teacher Dashboard, where the available modules can be selected according to the task to be performed.

For academic record management, the Teacher selects the appropriate class, subject, and grading term before uploading the Official DepEd Electronic Class Record (ECR). The system validates the uploaded file to ensure that the required information is properly recognized and processed. If errors are detected, the Teacher is prompted to correct and reupload the file. Once validation is successful, the system automatically processes the academic records and applies the predefined academic risk classification criteria to determine learners' current-term academic risk levels and identify weak-performing subjects. The Teacher may also view available advisory Random Forest predictions of learners' academic risk levels for individual subjects in the succeeding grading term. These predictions are presented separately from the current-term rule-based classifications and serve as supplementary information for academic monitoring.

For reading assessment, the Teacher records the applicable Group Screening Test (GST) results and individual reading assessment results when indicated. The system supports the organization and monitoring of learners' reading performance and intervention progress across the Beginning-of-School-Year (BOSY), Middle-of-School-Year (MOSY), and End-of-School-Year (EOSY) assessment periods. Reading-related assessment and intervention follow the applicable assessment procedures and remain separate from academic risk classification and Random Forest prediction.

The workflow also includes academic intervention monitoring, where the Teacher reviews identified learner needs and available draft intervention recommendations or Personalized Learning Plans (PLPs). The Teacher may document intervention activities, observations, and learner progress to support continuous monitoring. In the Lesson Plan Management module, the Teacher submits lesson plans for review by the School Principal. Approved submissions are recorded in the system, while those returned with feedback may be revised and resubmitted. Additionally, the Teacher can generate and review authorized academic and monitoring reports.

Overall, the workflow demonstrates how CNHS LEARN supports teachers in managing academic information, identifying learners who may require additional support, documenting interventions, and completing instructional and reporting responsibilities through a centralized system.

**Development and Testing**  
**Test Cases**  
Test cases refer to a series of tests carried out in order to determine if the system works as it should based on the requirements. The test case aims at checking whether the particular aspect of the system gives the required output. 

**Table 7\. Test Cases for Admin System**

| TEST ID | Test Case | Test Data | Expected Result |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| ADM-01 | Verify admin can access the system through valid login | Valid admin email and password | Admin is successfully logged in and redirected to the admin dashboard |
| ADM-02 | Verify system rejects invalid admin login credentials | Invalid email or wrong password | System shows an authentication error and denies access |
| ADM-03 | Verify inactive admin account cannot log in | Deactivated admin account | System blocks login and shows an inactive-account message |
| ADM-04 | Verify teacher cannot access admin portal pages | Valid teacher account visiting /dashboard | System redirects the teacher away from admin pages |
| ADM-05 | Verify admin dashboard loads summary analytics | Logged-in admin with existing school data | Dashboard displays KPI cards and analytics without errors |
| ADM-06 | Verify admin can view user management list | Existing teacher and admin accounts | User Management shows registered users with roles and status |
| ADM-07 | Verify admin can view user management list | Existing active teacher account | Account status changes and deactivated user can no longer log in |
| ADM-08 | Verify admin can create a teacher account | Valid teacher name, email, and role | New teacher account is saved successfully and appears in User Management |
| ADM-09 | Verify admin can edit teacher account information | Existing teacher account with updated valid information  |  Updated teacher account information is saved successfully |
| ADM-10 | Verify required fields are enforced in user management | Missing email or role | System shows validation and does not save incomplete data |
| ADM-11 | Verify system prevents duplicate user email addresses | Email address already registered  | System displays a duplicate-email error or prevents account creation |
| ADM-12 | Verify admin can reset a user’s password | Existing user account selected for password reset | Password reset is completed according to the system’s implemented reset procedure |
| ADM-13 | Verify admin can view and manage sections | Existing grade levels and sections | Sections page lists sections correctly and allows admin management actions |
| ADM-14 | Verify admin can create a section | Valid grade level and section name | New section is saved successfully and appears in the section list |
| ADM-15 | Verify required fields are enforced when creating or editing sections | Missing grade level or section name | System displays validation and prevents saving incomplete section information |
| ADM-16 | Verify system prevents duplicate sections | Existing section name under the same grade level | System prevents duplicate section registration and displays an appropriate message |
| ADM-17 | Verify admin can assign a class to a teacher | Teacher, subject, section, school year, and term | Class assignment is created and appears under the teacher’s My Classes |
| ADM-18 | Verify class assignment prevents incomplete records | Missing teacher or subject  | Shows a validation and does not create the assignment |
| ADM-19 | Verify admin can edit a class assignment without associated academic records | Existing class assignment without associated ECR records | Updated class assignment information is saved successfully |
| ADM-20 | Verify system prevents changes to class assignments with associated ECR records | Existing class assignment with an associated ECR workbook | System blocks the assignment change and displays a warning indicating that associated records already exist |
| ADM-21 | Verify admin can review submitted less plans | Lesson plan with status “Under review” | Lesson Plan Review shows the pending plan with teacher and class details |
| ADM-22 | Verify admin can approve a lesson plan | Pending Lesson plan | Plan status changes to Approved and teacher is notified |
| ADM-23 | Verify admin can return a lesson plan for revision | Pending lesson plan with remarks | Plan status changes to Needs Revision and teacher is notified |
| ADM-24 | Verify Academic Monitoring identifies learners requiring academic attention | Classes with imported ECR grades | Academic Monitoring displays learners requiring academic attention based on the system’s defined academic risk classification and shows the corresponding monitoring counts |
| ADM-25 | Verify admin can view Classroom Remedial recommendations for academic concerns | Class or subject with learners requiring academic support | System displays Classroom Remedial as an applicable academic intervention pathway for the identified class or subject |
| ADM-26 | Verify reading intervention records are based on applicable reading assessment evidence | Learners with available Phil-IRI assessment records and differing academic performance  | System displays reading intervention information based on available Phil-IRI assessment evidence and does not determine reading intervention solely from academic grades |
| ADM-27 | Verify Academic Monitoring values are consistent across views | Same academic monitoring dataset | Academic monitoring counts, subject grades, and applicable academic information are consistent across available summary and monitoring views |
| ADM-28 | Verify admin can filter monitoring records | Grade, section, subject, or quarter filter | Only matching student or class records are displayed |
| ADM-29 | Verify admin can search for a student in monitoring | Student name or learners number | Matching student record is displayed  |
| ADM-30 | Verify admin can open student monitoring details | Existing monitored student | Detailed view shows subject grade, risk level, and recommendation information |

**Implementation Plan** 

**Planning and Design**   
The planning and design phase focuses on defining the system needs, analysis processes, and workflows for the development of CNHS LEARN. The researchers created a data flow model that shows the centralization of learner records, the process of getting academic grades from the Official Department of Education Electronic Class Record (ECR), and the separation of academic performance monitoring and reading assessment monitoring processes. 

In Academic Monitoring, the system was designed on three grading terms: Term 1, Term 2, and Term 3\. The system uses completely and definitively assigned ECR grades to establish predefined criteria based on learners' current academic risks. The system categorises the learners' academic risk as High Risk (below 75), Moderate Risk (75 to 80\) and Low Risk (above 80). The Rule Based Section also highlights low performing subjects and provides recommendations for teacher review for Classroom Remediation. Students who have incomplete or unfinalized academic records will not be given a formal academic risk classification until necessary information is available.

A Random Forest Classifier is an independent experimental predictive analytics. The classifier does not make a statement about the current academic risk, but rather about the potential changes in academic performance for each of the individual subjects in the term following. This classifies anticipated performance patterns as Improving, Stable, or Declining. And only forecasts for transitioning from Term 1 to Term 2 and Term 2 to Term 3 are produced and only until Term 2\. The predictions are considered additional early-warning information, and do not replace the academic risk classifications used in the system or automatically assign interventions.

In ARAL Reading Monitoring, an independent evaluation process that is not based on ECR grades or Random Forest predictions. Learners are administered English and Filipino Group Screening Test (GST) at the Beginning of the School Year (BOSY). If a learner's screening score is below the agreed upon cut-off point at 28/40, the learner is identified for further assessment using the Form 3 Individual Reading Assessment. The individual assessment is in the form of evidence that will be used to determine reading levels of Independent, Instructional and Frustration reading levels, as per applicable assessment procedures. Monitoring and reassessment of learners' reading progress are supported with Middle of School Year (MOSY) and End of School Year (EOSY) assessments. The ongoing, completion or referral of reading interventions continue to be dependent upon evidence of assessment, school procedure and authorized personnel.the process does not depend on ECR grades or random forest predictions. At the Beginning of the School Year (BOSY), covered learners take the English and Filipino Group Screening Test (GST). Learners who score below the set threshold (currently planned at 28/40) undergo the Form 3 Individual Reading Assessment, which classifies them as Independent, Instructional, or Frustration readers. At the Middle of the School Year (MOSY), learners receiving support are reassessed to decide whether they exit or continue the intervention. At the End of the School Year (EOSY), a final reading progress review and further support recommendations are made. The specific GST thresholds and exit criteria remain subject to school confirmation. Reading-focused draft PLPs may be generated at BOSY even before Term 1 grades are available. 

The system's intervention-support process draws on the predetermined academic rules and results from the reading assessment(s) to provide suggestions for a draft Personalized Learning Plan (PLP). These recommendations contribute to the identification of the needs of learners and the possible academic support actions and the need for keeping track of the interventions. They are not automatically approved or complete plans of instruction. The recommendations are reviewed by the teacher, the teacher figures out what intervention activity to use to remediate, and the teacher tracks the progress of the student in the remedial activity, and the School Principal oversees school-wide academic performance, the intervention activity, and applicable reading intervention referrals.

This stage ensures that requirements, workflows, and functions are properly planned and designed before development, minimizing errors and major revisions in later stages.

**Development and Prototyping Phase**  
The system will be developed as a modern web application using HTML, CSS, [Next.js](http://Next.js), React, and Javascript for the application layer, with Supabase (PostgreSQL) as the backend for data storage, authentication, and row-level security. The system includes user authentication and role-based access control for the principal/administrator and teachers, with learners accessing relevant learning support information or active plans based on implemented permissions.

The implementation of academic record management, ECR based grade processing, SF2 attendance monitoring, learner information management, academic analytics, reading assessment monitoring, intervention support and report generation were some of the features implemented in the development process. The ECR processing was developed to ensure that information from academics is accurate and that the information currently stored in the learner's site record is accurate. The academic record workflow separates draft and final/published academic records, while the term-based restrictions are designed to maintain academic records from previous terms and to ensure that records are not altered without authorization and/or unintentionally.

The rule based component was incorporated to determine the current academic risk classifications based on completed and finalized academic grades, to identify weak subject performance and to make draft Classroom Remediation recommendations. A separate assessment process based on Phil-IRI was used to implement assessment and decisions about intervention for reading. These processes provide independent sources of assessment evidence, and do not depend on predictions from Random Forest.

In Random Forest, a Python-based model was created with the help of the scikit-learn library and the FastAPI service was set up to facilitate the model's inference. Synthetic academic records were used in training and testing the model with a structure based on the DepEd ECR grading system. It uses nine academic input factors as a basis for predicting the likely subject performance trend in the next grading period. This prediction is given as an additional information tool for decision making and not as an academic risk classification.

The system also includes recommendations for draft Personalized Learning Plans and features for monitoring interventions to help authorized school staff analyze learner needs and allocate academic support. Reading assessment information (including relevant GST and Form 3 results and BOSY, MOSY and EOSY monitoring records) is kept separately to academic risk analysis. The attendance records generated by processing SF2 are also used for attendance monitoring and reporting, and are not used in the inputs to the Random Forest model and academic risk classification.

The user interface was created with re-usable, component-based pages, offering role-specific dashboards, class and learner record views, academic performance indicators, reports, notifications and intervention-monitoring screens. The School Principal can access school-wide administrative and monitoring functions while the teacher performs records and academic activity in the scope of their assignment. A prototype of a Student Portal was also created but not planned to be used in operation.

The researchers continuously improved the modules, human interfaces and data-processing steps of the system through iterative Agile development. The revisions were made to be more consistent with the functionality, usability, data security and consistency with academic and administration practices of Cambaog National High School.

**Testing and Feedback Phase**  
After development, the system will be tested for functionality, performance, and security. The researchers evaluated the system through unit testing, functional testing, integration testing, and regression testing to ensure its core modules such as academic record management, E-Class Record (ECR) importing and validation, rule-based academic risk classification, attendance monitoring, Phil-IRI reading assessment, intervention recommendations, draft Personalized Learning Plan (PLP) support, reporting, and role-based access control functioned properly. The testing process mainly aimed to detect error functional, consistency data, and interaction between interconnected modules.

	Academic record processing was of special concern for accuracy and integrity. The tests that were conducted related to the ECR included tests of the validity of the learner records, restriction of grading terms, repeated import, incomplete grade handling, and protection from unintended changes to existing academic records. The rule-based algorithms were evaluated with respect to a set of predefined academic risk criteria based on complete and finalized ECR grades, whereas the Random Forest Classifier was evaluated computationally by synthetic academic records and learner-grouped testing. The next-term subject performance predictions from the classifier remained as separate advice and would not be taken into account as part of the official academic classification and decision to intervene. The Phil-IRI reading assessments and the SF2 attendance monitoring were also analyzed separately, to maintain their different assessment and reporting processes.

	The developed system has been evaluated with the identified respondents with the help of structured evaluation instruments for feedback. The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) was employed to evaluate the perceptions of participating teachers and the School Principal regarding the Perceptions of Usefulness, Perceived Ease of Use and Behavioral Intention to Use of the technology. Furthermore, the system's software quality was assessed by the involved IT faculty members and IT experts based on the relevant characteristics of ISO/IEC 25010:2023. The evaluation results provided data about the perceived acceptability of the system and software quality, and identified issues and observations that led to further refinement of the system functionality, usability and data management processes.

**Deployment and Implementation Phase**  
The system will be implemented in the school after being tested successfully. The system will be deployed using Vercel, and was later set up with a custom .com domain to offer a dedicated web address for authorized users within the school premises. The web application hosting platform was still Vercel, and centralized database management and authentication services were still being provided by Supabase. The deployment activities involved configuring the environment, connecting it to the database, managing user accounts and setting up permissions based on roles for the School Principal and teachers.

Authorized teachers were given functionalities for importing existing information on learners and their academic records in supported file formats during implementation. When uploading records, teachers can choose the grading term from the E-Class Record (ECR) import workflow. All imported data are validated in order to save learner information, class assignments, subjects, school years and grading terms as draft for the teacher's review and publication. Academic levels for learners are determined and subject areas identified as weak according to a set of rules based on the finalised academic grades. When detailed academic data is available, the Random Forest Classifier offers additional experimental predictions for the trends of individual subjects for the subsequent grading term, classified as Improving, Stable or Declining. The system also provides draft recommendations for a Personalized Learning Plan (PLP) for teachers to review and plan for intervention.

Reading assessment is done individually by using the appropriate procedures in the Philippine Informal Reading Inventory (Phil-IRI), such as recording and monitoring the reading assessment results and the progress of learners. Eligibility, referral and placement in Formal ARAL Summer Program is not within the scope of this system. School Form 2 (SF2) attendance records are kept separately for attendance monitoring and reporting purposes and are not part of academic risk classification or Random Forest forecasting.

The deployed system will be monitored and verified to gauge system stability, access, data integrity and correct user access permissions. Additional testing and refinement can be performed to overcome any technical problems that were identified, and to enhance usability and to keep the system in line with the academic and administrative needs at Cambaog National High School.

**Post Deployment Evaluation Phase**

The final phase will evaluate the developed system in terms of software quality and user acceptance. Software quality will be assessed using the ISO/IEC 25010:2023 model and the quality characteristics included in the study’s evaluation instrument, as applicable. These may include functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, interaction capability, reliability, security, maintainability, flexibility, and safety.

User acceptance will be evaluated through structured questionnaires based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). The Principal and participating teachers will assess the system in terms of perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and behavioral intention to use.

The collected responses will be tabulated and analyzed using appropriate statistical tools, including percentage distribution and weighted mean, as specified in the research methodology. The results will be used to assess the software quality and user acceptance of CNHS LEARN as a decision-support system for academic monitoring, reading progress monitoring, and personalized intervention planning at Cambaog National High School.

 **Chapter IV**

**RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS**

**Results of the Preliminary Study **

A preliminary study was conducted at Cambaog National High School (CNHS) through client interviews, observations, and requirements-gathering sessions with the School Principal and teachers. The study examined the school's existing practices in managing academic and attendance records, monitoring learner performance, identifying learners requiring academic support, implementing interventions, and preparing reports. The findings revealed operational challenges affecting the efficiency of school data management, academic monitoring, and intervention processes.

The preliminary study results were used to identify the existing issues in the school and translate the issues into functional requirements for the proposed CNHS LEARN: A Centralized School Data Analytics System Using Random Forest and Rule-Based Algorithms for Personalized Learning Plan Generation. Table 9 presents the identified problems, their effects on existing school operations, and the corresponding system functionalities developed to address them. 

**Table 9\. Identified Problems, Proposed System Features, and Corresponding Solutions**

| Identified Problem at CNHS | Affected Operations | System Functional Resolution |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| The submission of the Official DepEd E-Class Record is done manually or through group chats, making file management inefficient.  | Retrieving, organizing, and consolidating submitted ECR files require additional time and effort from teachers and the Principal.  | Official E-Class Record Upload – Centralizes the submission, organization, and retrieval of ECR files.  |
| Academic records are scattered across different files, making them difficult to retrieve and monitor.  | Teachers must access multiple files to review learner grades, retrieve academic information, and monitor performance.  | Academic Records Management – Organizes learner academic records in a centralized platform for easier searching, filtering, and monitoring.  |
| Identifying learners who require intervention is time-consuming because it is done manually.  | Teachers must individually examine class-subject grades to identify academically at-risk learners and their weak-performing subjects.  | Academic Risk Classification – Identifies learners’ academic risk levels using finalized class-subject grades obtained from the Official DepEd E-Class Record (ECR) |
| There is no standardized basis for recommending learner interventions  | Teachers may encounter difficulties in consistently identifying suitable intervention strategies based on learners' academic needs.  | Rule-Based Recommendation – Uses predefined rules and identified academic needs to suggest intervention pathways for teacher review and selection.  |
| ARAL-related assessment intervention records are maintained in separate spreadsheets, making monitoring and coordination inconsistent. | Reviewing reading assessment results, coordinating referrals and facilitator assignments, and monitoring reading interventions require checking separate records.  | ARAL Monitoring – Centralizes reading assessment records, referrals, facilitator assignments, intervention status, and learner progress based on applicable assessment evidence and school procedures.  |
| Monitoring the progress of learner interventions is difficult.  | Tracking intervention status, learner progress, and teacher observations requires reviewing and updating separate records.  | Learner Intervention Monitoring – Tracks intervention status, learner progress, and teacher remarks within the system.  |
| Lesson plans are submitted and reviewed manually through face-to-face transactions or group chats.  | Lesson plan submission, review, feedback, revision, and approval require manual coordination between teachers and the Principal.  | Lesson Plan Management – Supports digital submission, review, feedback, revision, and approval of lesson plans.  |
| Preparing reports every grading period is time-consuming.  | Teachers and the Principal must manually consolidate academic and intervention information when preparing periodic reports.  | Reports Module – Generates exportable academic and intervention reports to support school reporting.  |

Table 9 presents the operational challenges identified during the preliminary study at Cambaog National High School and their effects on existing school processes. The findings revealed difficulties in academic record submission and retrieval, manual identification of learners requiring academic support, inconsistent intervention planning and monitoring, fragmented ARAL-related records, manual lesson plan management, and time-consuming report preparation. These challenges increased the effort required to organize learner information, monitor academic performance, coordinate interventions, and accomplish administrative tasks.

To address these concerns, CNHS LEARN incorporates the Official DepEd E-Class Record Upload, Academic Records Management, Academic Risk Classification, Rule-Based Recommendation, ARAL Monitoring, Learner Intervention Monitoring, Lesson Plan Management, and Reports modules. These functionalities provide a centralized environment for managing academic records, identifying learners who may require support, recommending intervention pathways for teacher review, monitoring intervention progress, managing lesson plan workflows, and generating reports. Together, they support more organized academic monitoring and school-level decision-making.

**Results and Discussion of the Random Forest Model Evaluation**

This subsection presents the evaluation results of the trained Random Forest classifier described in Chapter 3\. The model was developed and evaluated using synthetic academic records and was designed to generate advisory academic risk predictions categorized as High Risk, Moderate Risk, and Low Risk. These predictions provide supplementary analytical information for authorized school personnel when reviewing learner performance and identifying learners who may require additional attention. They do not replace the rule-based academic risk classifications derived from finalized E-Class Record (ECR) grades or automatically determine intervention eligibility.

The evaluation dataset consisted of 3,600 synthetic academic term records representing 1,200 simulated learners across three grading terms. The model used 13 numeric academic input features, comprising eight subject-grade variables and five derived academic indicators. The target variable, risk\_label, was generated from each synthetic learner record's General Weighted Average (GWA), with values below 75 categorized as High Risk, values from 75 to 84 as Moderate Risk, and values of 85 or above as Low Risk. Although GWA was used to derive the target labels, it was excluded from the model's input features.

The dataset was divided through a stratified 80:20 row-level train–test split, allocating 2,880 synthetic records for training and 720 records for holdout testing. A separate five-fold stratified cross-validation procedure was conducted using the complete synthetic dataset of 3,600 records.

**Table 10\. Random Forest Model Evaluation Results on Synthetic Academic Records**

| Evaluation Measure | Result |
| ----- | ----- |
| Synthetic records | 3,600 (1,200 simulated learners x 3 terms) |
| Input features | 13 numeric academic indicators |
| Training/holdout split | 2,880 / 720 records (80:20 stratified, row-level) |
| Holdout accuracy | 99.17% |
| Holdout macro recall | 98.82% |
| Holdout macro F1-score | 98.99% |
| Five-fold cross-validation mean accuracy | 98.42% ± 0.44 percentage points |
| Five-fold cross-validation mean macro F1 | 98.10% ± 0.54 percentage points |

As presented in Table 10, the Random Forest classifier achieved a holdout accuracy of 99.17%, correctly classifying 714 of the 720 synthetic academic term records in the testing partition. The model also obtained a macro precision of 99.17%, macro recall of 98.82%, and macro F1-score of 98.99%. These results indicate that the classifier was able to reproduce the GWA-derived academic risk categories with high classification performance within the synthetic holdout dataset.

The separate five-fold stratified cross-validation produced a mean accuracy of 98.42%, with a standard deviation of approximately 0.44 percentage points, and a mean macro F1-score of 98.10%, with a standard deviation of approximately 0.54 percentage points. The macro F1-score provides a balanced summary of classification performance across the three academic risk categories by assigning equal importance to each category. These findings further describe the model's performance across different partitions of the synthetic development dataset.

However, the reported results should be interpreted within the limitations of the model development and evaluation procedures. The dataset consisted entirely of artificially generated academic records, and actual individual historical ECR records from Cambaog National High School were not used for model training or offline evaluation. Consequently, the reported metrics do not establish predictive accuracy on actual CNHS learner records.

Furthermore, the train–test partitioning and cross-validation procedures were conducted at the academic term-record level rather than at the unique learner level. As a result, multiple term records belonging to the same simulated learner could appear across different partitions, introducing a potential learner-level information leakage concern and possibly producing optimistic estimates of model generalization.

Another limitation concerns the relationship between the model's input features and its training target. Although GWA was excluded from the 13 predictor variables, the target labels were derived from GWA, while the input features consisted of subject grades and grade-derived academic indicators. Therefore, the reported performance primarily demonstrates the model's ability to reproduce grade-based academic risk patterns within the synthetic dataset rather than independently predict future academic outcomes.

Within CNHS LEARN, the trained Random Forest classifier provides supplementary advisory academic risk predictions that remain separate from the rule-based academic risk classifications used in the academic monitoring workflow. The rule-based component applies predefined academic risk classification criteria to finalized ECR grades, while weak-performing subjects and draft intervention guidance are identified through separate predefined academic rules.

The resulting information supports authorized teachers and the School Principal in reviewing learner performance and determining appropriate follow-up actions. Reading-related concerns require applicable assessment evidence and authorized review before ARAL-related intervention decisions are made. Attendance monitoring also operates independently and is not included among the Random Forest input features.

Overall, the evaluation findings demonstrate that the Random Forest classifier achieved high classification performance on the synthetic academic development dataset. Nevertheless, learner-grouped validation and further evaluation using appropriately authorized actual learner records would be necessary before establishing the model's generalization performance in operational school settings.

**Results and Discussion of the System’s Evaluation**

A comprehensive system evaluation was performed to systematically evaluate the quality, functionality, and user acceptance of the developed CNHS LEARN: A Centralized School Data Analytics System Using Random Forest and Rule-Based Algorithms for Personalized Learning Plan Generation. The two models used for the evaluation were the ISO/IEC 25010 Software Product Quality Model to evaluate the technical quality of the system, and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to evaluate the acceptance of the system by users in terms of Perceived Usefulness, Perceived Ease of Use, and Behavioral Intention to Use.

A total of twenty-one (\$N \= 21\$) respondents participated in the evaluation, comprising Faculty Evaluators, IT Experts, and Stakeholders. Weighted Mean was used to analyze the responses, and the five-point Likert Scale was used to interpret the responses. The respondent distribution is presented in Table 11, while the interpretation scale is presented in Table 12\.** **

**Table 11\. Distribution and Profile of the Evaluation Respondents **

Table 11 shows the distribution and profile of the respondents who participated in the evaluation of the developed system. The respondents for the study were twenty-one (21), comprising five (5) Faculty Evaluators, five (5) IT Experts, and eleven (11) Stakeholders. The stakeholder group consisted of one (1) Principal and ten (10) Teachers as the intended end users of the developed system. These responding groups provided broad coverage from the academic, technical, and operational points of view.

**Table 12\. Likert Scale**

| Mean Range | Scale Weight | Range | Descriptive Evaluation |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **4.21 – 5.00 ** | 5 | Highly Acceptable | The system fully satisfies the evaluation criteria and demonstrates excellent quality, functionality, and usability with minimal or no improvements required.  |
| **3.41 – 4.20 ** | 4 | Acceptable | The system meets the required evaluation criteria and performs effectively, although minor improvements may further enhance its quality. |
| **2.61 – 3.40 ** | 3 | Moderately Acceptable | The system demonstrates acceptable performance but requires several improvements to better satisfy the evaluation criteria.  |
| **1.81 – 2.60 ** | 2 | Fairly Acceptable | The system only partially meets the evaluation criteria and requires significant improvements in functionality and usability.  |
| **1.00 – 1.80 ** | 1 | Not Acceptable | The system fails to satisfy the evaluation criteria and requires major revisions before it can be considered acceptable.  |

***Legends:** 5 \= Highly Acceptable, 4 \= Acceptable, 3 \= Moderately Acceptable, 2 \= Fairly Acceptable, 1 \= Not Acceptable*

**Figure 37\. Weighted Mean Formula**

| Weighted Mean \= x ∑(f⋅x)​ N |
| :---: |

In evaluating the developed system, the five-point Likert scale with the corresponding descriptive interpretation is displayed in Table 12, and the weighted mean formula is displayed in Figure 37, which shows the computation of the average evaluation scores from the respondents. The weighted mean scores were calculated, and then the range of mean values for each evaluation criterion was used to interpret the scores and indicate acceptability. The results of the system evaluation were used to interpret the results based on two software quality models: ISO/IEC 25010 Software Product Quality Model and Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). The Evaluation Outcomes from the Faculty Evaluators, IT experts, and the Stakeholders are then presented and discussed.

**CHAPTER V**

**Summary of Findings**

This study aimed to develop CNHS LEARN, a centralized web-based school data analytics system using Random Forest and Rule-Based algorithms to support academic monitoring and personalized learning intervention planning at Cambaog National High School (CNHS). The system was developed to address challenges associated with fragmented academic and attendance records, time-consuming monitoring procedures, identification of learners requiring academic assistance, and the organization of intervention-related information.

Based on the development and evaluation results presented in Chapter IV, the following findings were established:

1.  Centralized Management of Academic and Attendance Records  
   The developed CNHS LEARN system provided a centralized platform for managing learners' academic and attendance information. Its features included academic record uploading and management, class and section monitoring, attendance recording, learner information retrieval, and report generation. The system supported authorized teachers and the School Principal in accessing relevant school records through role-based interfaces.  
   The system also provided attendance monitoring functions for assigned class advisers, including the recording of morning and afternoon attendance sessions. These functions supported the organization and retrieval of attendance information while maintaining attendance monitoring as a process separate from academic risk prediction.  
2. Academic Performance Monitoring and Rule-Based Risk Classification  
   The system utilized finalized class-subject grades from the Official DepEd E-Class Record (ECR) to identify weak-performing subjects and classify learners according to predefined academic risk levels. Learners with grades below 75 were categorized as High Risk, those with grades from 75 to 80 as Moderate Risk, and those with grades above 80 as Low Risk. Learners without the required grade information were not automatically assigned an academic risk classification.  
   Through the Academic Monitoring module, authorized teachers and the School Principal could review learners' academic performance, identify areas requiring attention, and examine intervention-related information. The system also supported the preparation of draft Personalized Learning Plans (PLPs) and the monitoring of intervention progress, subject to review by authorized school personnel.  
3.  Random Forest Model Evaluation  
   The Random Forest model was developed as a supplementary academic decision-support component for predicting learners' academic risk categories. The model was evaluated using 3,600 synthetic academic records representing 1,200 simulated learners across three grading terms.  
   The evaluation produced a holdout accuracy of 99.17% using 720 synthetic test records. Separate five-fold stratified cross-validation yielded a mean accuracy of 98.42%, with a standard deviation of 0.44 percentage points, and a mean macro F1-score of 98.10%, with a standard deviation of 0.54 percentage points.  
   These findings demonstrated strong predictive performance within the synthetic evaluation dataset. However, the results did not establish equivalent performance on actual CNHS learner records. The model's predictions remained supplementary to the official rule-based academic risk classification and did not independently determine learner intervention assignments.  
4. User Acceptance Based on the Technology Acceptance Model  
   The developed system was evaluated by ten teachers and one School Principal using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), covering Perceived Usefulness, Perceived Ease of Use, and Behavioral Intention to Use.  
   The stakeholder evaluation obtained an overall composite mean of 4.90, interpreted as Highly Acceptable. The findings indicated favorable perceptions of the system's usefulness, ease of use, and potential for continued utilization in academic monitoring and school-related decision-making.  
5. Software Quality Evaluation Based on ISO/IEC 25010:2023  
   The software quality of CNHS LEARN was evaluated by five IT Faculty members and five IT Experts based on the nine quality characteristics of ISO/IEC 25010:2023: Functional Suitability, Performance Efficiency, Compatibility, Interaction Capability, Reliability, Security, Maintainability, Flexibility, and Safety.  
   The IT Faculty evaluation obtained an overall composite mean of 4.82, while the IT Expert evaluation obtained an overall composite mean of 4.62. Both results were interpreted as Highly Acceptable.

These findings indicated that the evaluators generally assessed the developed system favorably in relation to the specified software quality characteristics. Nevertheless, the evaluation results represented the assessments of the participating respondents and did not independently establish long-term operational performance or the effectiveness of the system in improving learners' academic outcomes.

**Conclusion**

Based on the findings of the study, the following conclusions were drawn:

1. CNHS LEARN provides a centralized environment for managing academic records, attendance information, learner monitoring activities, and school reports. Its implemented functions address the study's objective of organizing relevant school information within a single web-based platform for authorized teachers and the School Principal.  
2. The system supports academic monitoring by applying predefined grade-based criteria to identify weak-performing subjects and classify learners according to academic risk levels. The resulting information provides a consistent reference for identifying learners who may require academic support and reviewing appropriate intervention needs.  
3. The Random Forest model demonstrates promising predictive performance within the synthetic dataset used for its evaluation. Its integration provides an additional source of academic risk information; however, its outputs remain advisory and do not replace official grade-based classifications, applicable reading assessment procedures, or the professional judgment of teachers and the School Principal.  
4. The favorable Technology Acceptance Model evaluation indicates that the participating teachers and School Principal perceive CNHS LEARN as useful and manageable for its intended academic monitoring and decision-support functions. These findings support its potential for adoption within the school's defined operational setting.  
5. The Highly Acceptable ratings obtained from IT Faculty members and IT Experts indicate favorable assessments of the system's software quality based on the nine ISO/IEC 25010:2023 characteristics examined in the study.

Overall, the study achieved its development objective by producing a centralized web-based academic monitoring and decision-support system for Cambaog National High School. CNHS LEARN provides organized academic information, rule-based academic risk identification, supplementary Random Forest predictions, and intervention-monitoring support. Nevertheless, the system is intended to assist rather than replace authorized school personnel in making academic and intervention-related decisions. Its longer-term effectiveness and the predictive performance of its Random Forest model on actual learner data require further evaluation.

**Recommendations**

Based on the findings and limitations of the study, the following recommendations are proposed:

1. For Cambaog National High School  
   The school should consider the continued use and gradual implementation of CNHS LEARN for centralized academic record management, academic monitoring, attendance monitoring, and intervention documentation. Appropriate training and orientation should be provided to authorized teachers and the School Principal to promote consistent use of the system's functions.  
   The school should also establish procedures for verifying uploaded academic records, maintaining accurate attendance information, reviewing intervention recommendations, and updating learner progress records. Regular database backups, account management, and access-permission reviews should be conducted to support the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of learner information.  
2. For Teachers and the School Principal  
   Authorized school personnel should continue to review academic risk classifications, Random Forest advisory predictions, and draft intervention recommendations before determining appropriate learner support. Teachers should consider learners' actual academic performance, applicable Phil-IRI reading assessment results, classroom observations, and relevant school procedures when planning interventions.  
   Intervention records and learner progress should be updated regularly to support follow-up monitoring and school-level decision-making.  
3. For Future System Developers  
   Future developers should enhance the system's data validation, reporting, and monitoring capabilities based on feedback from authorized users. Improvements may include more comprehensive academic progress visualizations, enhanced intervention follow-up features, and additional safeguards for handling sensitive learner information.  
   Based on the recommendations provided by the system evaluators, further enhancements may include implementing detailed audit trails to track changes made to important learner records and identify the personnel responsible for such modifications; expanding existing academic monitoring alerts to notify authorized teachers of declining academic performance, repeated low assessment results, and frequent absences; allowing direct editing of lesson plans for minor revisions; enhancing comparative passing rate reports across grading periods; and improving school year management to initialize new academic records while preserving previous school year information for authorized reference.  
   Future development should also consider the scalability, maintainability, and reliability of the system as the volume of academic and attendance records increases.

4. For Future Random Forest Model Development  
   Future researchers and developers should evaluate the Random Forest model using appropriately authorized, de-identified actual learner academic records, subject to applicable data privacy requirements and school approval. The model should be assessed using learner-level data partitioning to reduce the possibility of data leakage between training and testing sets.  
   Additional evaluation should examine classification performance across academic risk categories, the representativeness of the training data, and the model's performance when applied to new learner records. These steps may help determine whether the model's predictive performance extends beyond the synthetic dataset used in the present study.  
5. For Future Researchers  
   Future researchers may conduct longitudinal studies to assess how CNHS LEARN performs during sustained school operations and whether its use contributes to improvements in record-management efficiency, academic monitoring practices, and intervention follow-up.

Further studies may also explore the adaptability of the system to other educational institutions while considering differences in grading procedures, administrative requirements, learner populations, and applicable education policies.
